Longineu Parsons

Longineu Parsons is a versatile trumpet player, comfortable in big bands, jazz combos, and classical ensembles. He has performed with Cab Calloway, Archie Shepp, and Branford Marsalis, and is passionate about preserving the legacy of Louis Armstrong.
Longineu was interviewed via Zoom on February 17, 2026 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and I’m very pleased to have Longineu Parsons with me this morning. Welcome, sir.
Oh thank you very much, Monk. Great to be here.
You are down in Florida, is that correct?
Yes, yes. I am at Florida A&M University where I’m a full professor of trumpet and composition.
When you think of yourself over the years, with all the things you do, is there one thing that you first think of yourself as?

Yes. The temptation is to say the first thing is a trumpet player, but no, it’s the trumpet that I use for expressing who I really am, and what I am is a force against all of this disorder that we have as human beings. You know my thing is I’m a person who’s out here trying to leave the world better than I found it.
Through your music?
Yes. Using music as my tool, my main tool. But that’s been what my life has been about. I’ve been one about pushing forward and living a life of service and of love to my fellow humanity.
It feels like an uphill battle recently.
It certainly is.

Yeah. So when you write a composition, is there usually something specific that gets your attention and that you feel the need to work on something new and express your reaction to it? Or is it more of a general sense of America and the world?

Well it’s – the music may come from different things. It may be about something specific, it may be about just a feeling or it might be about a certain motif that came into my head, a certain little melody and then I might develop that. It just depends on the frame of mind, which is different from day to day. I don’t have one way of doing things.
Do you write different when you’re angry than when you’re not?

I try to keep anger out of it. I think that, so it’s difficult to answer that because I can’t see myself doing music while angry. I don’t see myself as being productive in any way by © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
being angry so anger is something when I feel it then I observe myself and decide that I’m not going to be angry because it doesn’t help anything.

I really like that answer. I think the reason it came to my mind is I’ve read over the years critics, authors etcetera who listen to some of the music from the sixties when Coltrane and Archie Shepp etcetera were – for lack of a better term – they were playing pretty out. And sometimes you see the comment like, “What are they so angry about?” And I never talked to them but other people say this is not anger, this is something else.

Yeah, see I’m from that. That’s what really made me really decide to be a musician. Trane, and like that. And my dissertation was the jazz avant garde is the most representative art music to come from the United States in the late twentieth century.
Representative of what specifically?

The most representative art music. Period. It represents what American music has led to. If you look at it structurally, think about somebody who is really jazz interested and they’re black and they’re getting university training and it’s the fifties. What were they trained in? They’re interested in jazz so they’re playing that. But they are learning music theory, they’re learning Schoenberg, they’re learning Stravinsky. You know, like me, I mean I’m later but my education is all classical. So what would their music be like? It doesn’t have to stick to song form and being nice and stuff. And the struggle, yeah, the struggle is definitely in the music. I mean all these guys were buddies of mine. You know I can tell you we’ve had the discussions and I can tell you the music is out of love. Just because there’s a struggle doesn’t mean you have to be like – I mean yeah the anger is – there’s a certain amount of that that we all have to deal with. You know but anger is like – things like anger, jealousy and all these things that we might feel, these are real bad things. But it’s like a fire you know. If there’s just a little bit you know you can use the fire to heat your home, cook your food. But if it gets out of control it’ll burn your house down. So you know there’s a tinge of that, of the struggle, but it’s more like hey but you know this is spiritual. This is going beyond just oh I feel bad because of that – no, no, no this is hey, okay, here we come. You know? This is beautiful stuff. This is bringing people together. We look out in the audience and all kind of people are there together digging it. Hey.

And I’ve seen that in some of your live performances. I could feel the – even though I wasn’t in the room I could feel it between the audience and the stage. I had a – was fortunate to speak with Rashied Ali and I asked him a similar question but it was a little more directed towards, “Did the musicians at that time sit down and pre-discuss, ‘okay now we’re going to play more free, now we’re not going to be concerned with the form as much’ and so forth.” And he said, “No, it was a reflection of the times. We were © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
growing up in a different time than the beboppers. We loved that music but this was a different time.” I thought it was quite eloquent what he said.
Yeah. Rashied. Yeah if you shake his hand you feel like this is really a hand of steel there. Thoughtful dude, man. I always loved talking with him.

Was there a particular recording that – you’ve indicated that your training was mostly in European classical theory etcetera. Was there a particular jazz recording that you would consider like an AHA! moment?
Oh yeah. It was Coltrane, it was the album – what was it called – “Expressions.”
That’s a heck of a place to start.
Yeah, that was, I mean I had already stopped, I had already dropped out of pre-med, and told my parents I was going to be a musician.
How did that go?
They said they knew it all the time but they had to let me figure it out.
I see.
Because my father told me, he said, “You know it doesn’t matter that much what you do. What matters is whatever it is make sure you’re the best at it.”

So what did you think – I had an experience with Coltrane. I was into Paul Desmond and then Cannonball but someone said, “Oh you’ve got to listen to John Coltrane.” And unwittingly I went to a record store and I bought the LP called “Om” and it scared me at first. And I did not listen to him for a while until “My Favorite Things.” But what was it about “Expressions” that hit you in the heart?

The raw emotion and the freedom of it. He was free to express what he was feeling. He didn’t allow any of the so-called “rules” to get in the way. See when we are studying music, like as an academic I can tell you there’s rules this and rules that. And that’s B.S. There’s no such thing as a rule. These are performance practices. And then people came along and said this is the rule because if you’re doing Baroque music and Baroque counterpoint this is how J.S. Bach did it. Basically what they’re saying, “Therefore this is the rule.” Okay so we learn okay American song form. Okay the rules are like this. This chord means – suggests this scale or these potential scales, these chords. Okay so we learn these things and this is how it’s supposed to go. But these are somebody else’s inventions, somebody else saying this is how they do it. It’s good to know this, it’s good to be able to use this, but at the same time why do I need to be restricted to it? Because what if I want to employ say some of the twelve-tone work of Arnold Schoenberg that has spent plenty of time studying and learning how to do. You know as part of my final, my doctorate is in classical composition. My masters is in classical trumpet. But the masters is actually both and then the doctorate is composition but with trumpet as the side thing. So if I’m playing a tune like a regular jazz tune, which, you know most of the time © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

American song form from some show or whatever, okay, great song, great pieces of work. As a classical composer it’s not all that exciting to me. So I’m looking at how I can bring all of this together. And thinking about people like Henry Threadgill and thinking about people like Oliver Lake and the people I played with, well especially Cecil Taylor and Sun Ra. They’re looking for ways to do things, for new ways. Or finding ways to just express who they are. And why should that expression be restricted to what others have done before?

If you have a student trumpet player working on improvisation and they constantly are playing – well let’s say an F sharp over a B flat chord. Is there a difference between playing outside the chord if you do it on purpose or if you’re not aware that you’re doing it?

Okay outside the chord. Well if it’s a B flat what, let’s say if it’s a B flat seventh chord and you play an F sharp then you’re playing, okay we could say that’s flat sixth or flat thirteen. So where is that outside of the chord?
I had a feeling you were going to say that.
But there is a difference if you know what you’re doing and if you don’t.

Yeah, how can you tell with a student? I guess I’m thinking back on when, especially with junior high kids, trying to teach them to improvise and they keep playing a note that is a little bit advanced from them and I don’t feel that they know – right?
Oh yeah. That’s a wrong note then.
In that case it’s a wrong note I guess.

Yeah, yeah. Everything in context. But for me as a composer, these things, there are twelve tones in every octave. And so what we think of in classic theory is right notes and wrong notes, we think about devices – as modern composers we think about these things as devices for raising the tension of the music. But there are twelve tones in every octave. So you might have to start raising – maybe you want it nice and calm so you’re only going to use chord tones for a moment. But then you start using maybe extensions as it rises, but then maybe you need a good flat nine in there when it gets to a certain point, you know when it goes, you know when you’re taking it up you need these things to develop your arc of your music. If you look at classical compositions most of the time there’s an arc. It goes back to the Fibonacci numbers and all that. And so how are you going to construct your arc or whatever you’re going to do with it musically. And it’s these notes, these other – these notes that are not the regular chord tones that have a lot to do with it. I mean as we rise and we get the energy up we may need this big cluster where we [scats] and I mean a great example is film music you know where you have to express what’s going on on screen. You’re going to voice things a certain way if it’s a gentle scene where two people are speaking with each other gently who love each other or © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

whatever or something you know, something nice. And they you will use different things say if you have somebody holding a pistol on somebody. You’re going to need more tension in that music. So notes are going to be closer together, they’re going to be notes that are not necessarily what we think of as chord tones. But some people would say they’re outside but they’re actually, as a modern composer, there’s no outside.
Speaking of outside, do you think that you stand out from your classical colleagues because you’re also a jazz guy?

Okay I have to tell you the story. But the short answer is yes, is definitely yes. But see I was raising a kid myself, a son. I was in Jacksonville, Florida because I have family support there. And I was always just working at jazz, even though my undergrad stuff was classical too but I studied some at Berklee, but I was just playing jazz and knowing that I could play classical but thinking oh there’s nothing for me to do with that. So my son said to me, because I was on him about school, he said, “Well Dad, why don’t you go to school and learn something? You’re telling me about school and how important it is, what about you.” I said, “Well you know son, you’re right.” So I applied to the University of Florida for graduate school and they said, just told me, the guy told me on the phone, “Mr. Parsons, we don’t feel that you have the musical background to be successful in our legitimate music program.”
Ooh, legitimate.

He didn’t understand who he said that to. See I’m the guy who, in 1966 I was a part of integrating a public high school in Jacksonville, Florida, in redneck Jacksonville, Florida, in one of the most redneck areas in town. And I learned how to ignore certain problems and just push on with what I’m doing anyway. So, and how to push through when I needed to. And so I drove to Gainesville the next day, that next morning, and I went to his office first and I told him that I came to register. And you know to make a long story short, I ended up registering. I bullshitted my way with the composition professor, said, “Look” – well it’s not really bullshit. I said, “You know I haven’t studied composition before but I’ve been working in jazz music and I’ve been writing music and such, you know, and if I could just take a class as a post-baccalaureate you know. And he looked at my resume and he said, “Well of course you deserve a chance, so yeah, you come on.” In fact, and he was going to put me with another composition professor and then he changed his mind and decided he would teach me himself. And then the trumpet teacher, the same thing. I got in on to take not real graduate level classes but junior level classes in trumpet and composition. So about three weeks, a month in the trumpet teacher said, “Well you know I made a mistake. You need to be in my masters program.” And she said, “Let’s take care of this right now” and went to the dean’s office and the dean came out and said, © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
“Yeah but the composition professor has already been here and says he wants you in his program.
They were vying for your attention.
Yeah. So they said, “Well here at the University of Florida we know how to do it. Tell you what, you can do both and we’ll pay for it.” Because they were so apologetic for having treated me so badly.
Oh, that’s a terrific story.

But it goes on. Because when the – okay the trumpet teacher was still hard on me the whole time. I mean, but I didn’t realize it. I thought this was just the normal course of study. And then after I graduated the masters I was teaching at Florida A&M and everything. The trumpet teacher had a – well I sent a student there who was being treated very nicely. I started sending students there, my graduates. And then the trumpet teacher had a stroke and insisted that I be the one to replace her at the University of Florida. So I was there just teaching classical all day, and they were so nice, they said, “Okay we won’t insult you by having you teach freshmen and sophomores, you’ll teach only upper division and graduate students. Okay? And then so I talked with the dean of the music school about maybe since I’m hanging around there maybe I could do my doctorate, finish my doctorate, because I had already started the classes before I got the job at FAMU. I had started on the doctorate in composition. So anyway, I – while I was teaching there I started taking composition with the head composition guy just to kind of get acquainted, and the University of Florida accepts one person into a doctorate of composition program per year. Only one. And they accepted me. So I commuted from Tallahassee to Gainesville to do this. But what I’m getting at is, see I’m the guy who they said couldn’t do that, so therefore being the kind of butt hole that I am I had to make sure that I was the best at that, like my daddy said.
Well you set quite a role model for your son, who sort of initiated this, and you pushed through.
Yeah.

Well done. I was wondering if you experience what I did once. We’re used to writing jazz tunes, and the model is write a head, improvise on the form, and then play the head again. And I was struck by when I listened to the recording of “Mr. P.C.” by John Coltrane originally and I timed the melody and his melody took 11 seconds. And the recording is 7 minutes long. So when I try to write classical music, what I will call “classical,” I was struck by how long you work on something and you play it back and like wow, I have one minute so far, because everything has to be notated you know, it’s like where is this going? I got one minute and it took me a week.
It can be that way. Yeah. So I don't know if I understand what you’re asking me. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

I’m not asking a question, it’s really an observation, and I wondered if you had that experience of working on an ensemble piece or whatever, and thinking this is going really well but it’s still very short.

Mm hmm. Yeah well to me it’s always like that. That it takes quite a while for everything. But what I have found is that if I can have like a real lot of time to be devoted to the one thing then it gets faster as it goes. But to try to put in an hour or two here and there, I mean for me that first two hours is the warm up. That’s to get the mind ready to get where I was. But if I’m writing classical, I’m big into motific development. You know? So I’m into taking a little piece of this and seeing and doing all kinds of things with it.
Do you have a favorite instrumentation to write for?
No, but I do have a favorite composer.
And who would that be?

Dmitri Shostakovich. Since I was a kid, his music has spoken to me, and now as a quote unquote scholar or whatever I am, then I really appreciate his sense of motific development. He is the twentieth century Beethoven. You know [scats] think about how far that went with those four notes, three of them being the same notes, which actually came from a Haydn piano sonata by the way.
I did not know that.
Beethoven studied with Haydn in his quest to learn the pen of Mozart, as he put it.
I see.

And that’s from, and I mean if you listen to early Beethoven I mean it’s hard to tell that that’s not late Haydn, if you don’t know the piece, but of course everybody knows Beethoven, if you play the third, I mean who doesn’t know “Eroica.” But the first symphony, you know, most people don’t really know the first symphony. If you hear that, it’s a lot of Haydn.

Um hum. Well I’m struck by the length and the breadth of your experience, from Sun Ra to Shostakovich, and I don’t have a question here but it’s simply an observation that you don’t compartmentalize music, I guess, that’s my guess.

Yeah I think these lines that are placed between this and between that and all these things, these are artificial lines that people have placed. And that’s symbolic of the lines that we human beings place between each other in life, all over the world in all kinds of ways we have all of these lines that say I’m different from you. And that’s the biggest bunch of bullshit going in the world. You know this is what’s keeping us at war. This is what’s keeping us with all of this strife is that we make these lines instead of saying hey wait a minute, we don’t have to be that way. You know I’ve been blessed to be able to travel over a great part of the world. And I get to travel in a way so that I’m in places for © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

a while. I get to know people who live in places. And people are people when it comes down to it. And then we’re saying, “Oh yeah but I don’t like them because they’re like this and –” it’s crazy. I know of people in Paris where you have Iranian and Israeli making music together. Now this is an example of how we humans need to learn how to live. My production company is Tribal Disorder Productions. We’re a force against the disorder in the human tribe. I know humanity is a species, not a tribe, but I’m using tribe to say hey, it’s time for us to come together as one tribe. And we are, I think, at an existential state right now as far as where we are as humans getting along. Sun Ra always said that harmony, musicians are here to make harmony among people, to bring people together. And that’s what my life has been. Yeah. Like you said, Shostakovich to Sun Ra to Archie Shepp to, I came up in Cab Calloway’s band and playing shows and stuff, Broadway shows. So all of that, and really, before that I played the chitlin circuit playing R&B where that was really crazy, playing in places where they’re bootlegging the liquor you know.

You made it your business to know where the exits were, right? I love your description. It reminds me of fellas like Joe Wilder and the long trek through all these different kinds of gigs and developing a work ethic which is so important, and making yourself stand out so your phone rings.
Yeah, yes, yes. It’s a passion and someone who doesn’t love it shouldn’t mess with this.

Do you see that in your students? Does it occur to you – I remember Phil Woods said this thing, I’ll be very brief about it. He said you know if you’re thinking about being a jazz tenor player or a brain surgeon, be the brain surgeon and play tenor on the weekends.
Yeah.
You have to love it.
Agree with that completely.
Something you have to do is to be a musician. If you don’t have to then –
Do something else, that’s right. Do another thing.

Well I wanted to bring up a couple of people. First of all I was looking at your list of folks you’ve had associations with and my job is actually named after Joe Williams. I am the Joe Williams Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive, and he helped us get this project off the ground. Do you have memories with him?

Yeah, yes, yes. I do have memories of Joe Williams. I loved his whole style, his way of being on stage. I mean yeah he was something else. And see when I was coming up as a musician my mother always said, “You know I hope you get to –” she said her favorite singer was Joe Williams. So she was saying she would hope that maybe I would get to play with him someday, or know him or something like that. Or you know get to check him out live or something. So my mother was visiting me in New York and it happened © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

that Joe Williams was playing at a club there. So I said, “Hey Mom, we’re going out tonight.” And then she said, “Well where are we going?” I said, “You don’t worry about it,” you know, “just come on.” And then as we are getting ready she said, “Oh where is he playing?” She knew that that must have been why I was taking her out. So I said, “Yeah, okay you got it.” So I tipped the maître d – I guess he wouldn’t have been maître d – the waiter or the guy who met us there because – was it a restaurant? Yeah, maybe. I don’t even remember if it was just a bar. Yeah it must have been a restaurant with Joe Williams. So yeah anyway, I tipped him and said, “Look, my mother would really like to meet Joe Williams.” So I slid him a little bit of something, you know money, and then so then he went and took my mom up to meet Joe Williams there, and then the maître d came back to me and said, “Okay man, you can go back and meet him too if you want to.” So I went back and said hello. We all hung out, we had a nice little hang there.

Indeed. He was a classy guy. And he also was a good example, I’ve noticed with, I mentioned Joe Wilder, and Milt Hinton, they all had this thing that they were wonderful people, friendly. But at the same time they had so much pride in what they did, like don’t mess with that. Don’t disrespect what they do or you’ll be sorry. I mean they would react to something where they were being taken advantage of. They weren’t the kind of people that were just so nice that you could do anything and take advantage of them. They would not allow that.

Well we musn’t think that because somebody is nice that they can’t take care of themselves. In fact I think for my life I keep myself in very excellent physical condition and study martial arts since I was a teenager, and the point is to lead a gentle life, to be a nice person, to not have to be mean to people or to be like this or any of that kind of stuff. Be nice and loving. To not have to descend to somebody else’s level if they want to insult me or something like that. You know to be above all of these things.
The other name I wanted to bring up, and I know it’s dear to both of us, is the Adderleys.
Oh.

That’s what I say, oh. I just felt that Cannonball, for me, was it. He just exuded everything I wanted to be like a saxophone player, a spokesman, and then I got into their music, especially in the sixties, and eventually I was able to sit with Nat Adderley for an hour and it was a highlight of my life.
Really?
Yes.
Can I have a 30-second pause?
Yes.
Okay.
Are you going to tell me that that’s Nat Adderley’s horn? © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
That’s right. This is the one he did those recordings with Cannonball on.
Oh how did you end up with that?
The family wanted me to play it.
Oh.

Nat raised me as a musician. He and Cannonball knew my father when they were all here at Florida A&M as students. And see ‘cause when I started playing the horn, see my parents always had music in the house growing up. And my dad said, “Oh you’re playing the cornet, well you’ve got to hear Nat Adderley, that’s my buddy from school you know, and Cannonball Adderley and them. And so, and they were all part of the same social circles, you know all the doctor this and professor this and this and that and the other. You know so it was, “Yeah, if you’re going to play music, you listen to them.” And they played Duke Ellington for me all the time, well they played all the time, listening to Duke Ellington and Lionel Hampton and my mother liked Dinah Washington and Ella Fitzgerald and Sarah Vaughan and yeah, the Adderleys. And then what happened was when I came back to school to be a musician I was – well Cannonball and Nat would come in to do a concert at Florida A&M. And so I knew, I was waiting for them to come up, they were going to do like a little seminar during the day, before the concert. And so I knew they’d be coming up, so I could see them drive up so I could meet them, and I came up and said, “Oh, I know who you are” and all that. Because I’m junior, so I said “My name is Longineu.” “Oh yeah, oh okay yeah, uh huh. How’s your dad doing?” Yeah it was like that. And then Cannonball and Nat were speaking to us, the students in the recital hall and they played something. He had Hal Galper on piano and Roy McCurdy on drums. And a guy sitting next to me, another trumpet player in the band whose last name was McCurdy, he said, “I wonder if I’m related to him.” Turned out they are cousins. And so then Cannonball played something, Cannonball and Nat, and then they opened it up and said, “Okay well let’s see, hear the students play.” And they were surprised that we had a line of students who could really improvise but I went first. I pushed – I made sure I could play first. And I started playing and they were in the back doing like Cannonball and Nat would do, I’m sure it was something illegal, not to be talked about. And then I’m playing and then what I heard was, after I started playing Nat and Cannonball came back out to look to see what was going on, to see who is this playing. And Nat said, “Look you stick close to me” you know, “I’ll look out for you.” And he called my mother and told her the same thing and said, “Look, you don’t let him sign any contract without talking to me.”
Wow.

“And make sure,” he said, “A lawyer can make sure it’s legally binding but I know what it means in the business.” And he kept at it. And it was like that. And he told Nat Junior © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

and Alison, his two kids, he said, “Look, y’all have a brother, his name is Longineu, that’s my son too.” Well Nat had Bell’s Palsy. And so he lost the one side of his face, the feeling. So anyway it gradually got better, but he couldn’t play. He had me playing some stuff in his place, some of the gigs and stuff. And then, but when he could try to play the horn again it really wasn’t good, he had really lost it. And so I told him, “Nat,” you know, “there are things we can do to help you with that.” “Well no, the doctor told me that’s the best it’s going to get.” So I’m like I don’t care what the doctor said, I can help you. So he argued me down you know, because he was obstinate boy, Nat, you know, he was going to be right. So anyway I had a gig in St. Augustine and he was living in Lakeland so I called him up I said, “Nat, after my gig tonight, I’ll get off about” whatever “I get off at 1 A.M. I’m going to drive to Lakeland and then I’m going to give you these exercises that are going to straighten your lips out. And if it doesn’t work for you I’ll pay you for the lesson.” So he couldn’t say anything. He said, “All right, come on, come on.” So I went and we had breakfast and I gave him the exercises and I demonstrated how to use them and stuff like that. And then he gave me the highest compliment, he says, “Do you know what you are Longineu? Do you know what you are?” Oh goodness, what’s this. “Do you know what you are?” “No, Nat, what is that?” “You’re a motherfucker.”
High praise.

Yeah. So anyway so his wife Ann said, “Okay Longineu I’m going to make him do it, I’m going to make him do it.” So a couple of months later I’m on a gig in Orlando, in comes Nat Adderley holding his horn case. Now all before Nat had been telling me, you know, you don’t come and sit in on my gigs ‘cause you ain’t going to make no reputation on me [mumbles]. All out of love, you know, fun. So here he is coming up to me, “Hey man, can I sit in?” “What?” “Yeah.” “What is this?” So he came and pulled out his horn and he sounded like the old Nat Adderley. He wanted to show me that this did this for him.
Aw, bless your heart. I didn’t know any of that.

Yeah, because I was very much into learning about my embouchure, about how embouchure development is, and I had a buddy who, a close friend with this amazing range and I wanted to learn from him how he got it and he showed me the exercises from Carmine Caruso, ‘cause he studied with him for a long time. So I got, really, the benefit of Caruso training but without ever knowing Mr. Caruso.
Awesome.
You know and I gave the stuff to Nat and it worked. And I used the same stuff with all of my students. I’ve fixed many embouchures.
Oh, and you’ve played with Nat Junior?
